context_blurb:
Wind is air on the move, carrying the weather. It has one cause and one twist: the Sun warms Earth unevenly, and Earth's spin bends the moving air. A lawyer, an engineer, a balloon-watcher and a Norwegian father and son pieced it together.

Over a year the tropics soak up more solar energy than they lose to space, while the polar regions lose more than they gain. Winds and ocean currents carry heat toward the poles to keep the balance; a warm current gives its heat to the air, which is why a coast it washes has milder winters.

Air pressure is the push of the air's weight, and air flows from high pressure toward low. Air warmed at the equator rises, leaving low pressure below, while cold air sinks over the poles, piling up high pressure. So if Earth did not spin, the ground wind would blow straight from the poles toward the equator. The Sun's heating drives the wind, not Earth's spin, which only bends it.

The trade winds flow toward the equator to replace its rising air, yet north of it they blow from the northeast. Galileo had tied them to Earth's spin; in 1735 George Hadley, an English lawyer who preferred physics, showed how the spin turns air moving across it. Air arriving from the north lags behind the ground near the equator, which moves east fastest because it has the widest circle to cover each day, so Earth spinning beneath the moving air turns it into a northeast wind.

In 1835 the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis worked out the maths of spinning machines such as water wheels; others later applied it to Earth. Looking along a wind's path, the Coriolis effect turns it to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. The bend fades to nothing at the equator, and it is far too weak to steer a draining sink.

Air rising at the equator spreads poleward high up and sinks near 30 degrees, building belts of high pressure. From there, air heading for the equator becomes the trade winds. Air heading toward the pole is bent to its right, toward the east, so it blows from the southwest: the westerlies, filling the belt from 30 to 60 degrees north.

High above blow the jet streams, narrow rivers of fast wind 9 to 16 kilometres up. In the mid-1920s Wasaburo Ooishi tracked over 1,200 balloons through a surveyor's telescope called a theodolite and found fierce westerlies over Japan, strongest in winter: the first known evidence of a jet stream. Jets blow hardest where cold and warm air meet, and fastest when the difference is greatest. In winter the poles grow far colder while the tropics stay warm, so the poles and tropics differ most in temperature then.

B-29 bomber crews met the same winds over Japan in 1944, at some 320 kilometres an hour. Forecasters follow a jet stream because storms below tend to travel along its path: it is the main steering current for storms between the tropics and the poles.

During the First World War, with Europe's weather reports cut off, Vilhelm Bjerknes had weather stations built all over Norway. In Bergen he mapped the reports with his son Jacob. Sharp weather changes lay along boundaries between air masses, huge bodies of air each with its own temperature and dampness, and father and son named such a boundary a front, after the war's battle lines. The Bergen maps showed Norway's storms forming along the polar front, where cold polar air meets warm tropical air.

Cold air is denser than warm air, so the two do not easily mix, and the cold air stays low. At a cold front, cold air pushes under the warm air and forces it up steeply, so it cools fast into towering thunderclouds. At a warm front, the lighter warm air rides slowly up a gentle slope of cold air, spreading wide layers of cloud that give steady rain. Warm fronts also move about half as fast as cold ones, so the rain lasts for hours.

A barometer measures air pressure. In a low, an area of low pressure, air flows inward and rises, building clouds. So a falling barometer means a low is moving in, with rising air and storms; a fast fall often warns of rain or a gale. A rising barometer usually means a high, with sinking air and clear skies.
